power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Background: Although direct-acting antivirals have transformed hepatitis C virus (HCV) treatment, 25-30% of active infections in Spain remain undiagnosed.
We aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine-learning model to identify undiagnosed HCV infection using only data already recorded within the health system.
We conducted a retrospective, population-based cohort study using the Andalusian Population Health Database (BPS).
Individuals diagnosed with HCV between 2017 and 2024 (n=25,028) were matched, up to 10:1, to controls by birth year, sex, and health district.

An Explainable Boosting Machine was trained on 2017-2022 data, with a threshold set in a 2023 validation set to guarantee ≥60% sensitivity, then evaluated unmodified in an independent, non-matched, population-representative 2024 sample approximating real-world screening.
Predictors comprised chronic-disease diagnoses and laboratory summary statistics recorded ≥30 days before the index date; age and sex were excluded as matching variables.
Predictors reflecting socioeconomic proxies or matching artefacts (pharmaceutical co-payment category, a zone-level deprivation index) were removed after explainability review.

Results: In the independent test set, the model achieved an AUC of 0.837 (0.826 in validation), sensitivity 63.5%, specificity 91.8%, positive predictive value 7.0%, and negative predictive value 99.6%.
Leading predictors were minimum alanine.
Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection remains one of the principal preventable causes of chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma worldwide (Gamkrelidze et al., 2021).

text.text: The introduction of direct-acting antivirals (DAA) after 2015 transformed the therapeutic landscape, achieving cure rates above 95% (Zhang, 2016) and prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to establish the goal of eliminating viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030, including diagnosis of 90% of infected individuals and a 90% reduction in incidence (WHO, 2022).

text.text: As therapeutic effectiveness is no longer the principal limiting factor, case finding has become one of the central bottlenecks in the final phase of HCV elimination.

Spain is internationally recognized as one of the countries closest to these targets with the introduction of universal access to direct-acting antivirals and the implementation of the Strategic Plan for Tackling Hepatitis C, in 2015.

Since then, more than 172,000 patients have been treated with DAA, reducing the estimated national prevalence of active infection to approximately 0.14% (del Amo Valero et al., 2025; Romero Otero et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Since then, more than 172,000 patients have been treated with DAA, reducing the estimated national prevalence of active infection to approximately 0.14% <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(del Amo Valero et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Romero Otero et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Despite this progress, an estimated 25-30% of active infections remain undiagnosed, a proportion that has changed little in absolute terms since the baseline national seroprevalence survey of 2018, which already reported an undiagnosed fraction of 29.4% (Estirado Gómez et al., 2021; Thomadakis et al., 2026).

text.text: These remaining infections are increasingly concentrated among people who are not reached efficiently by conventional pathways targeting individuals under classical risk factors, including those with remote exposures, people who inject drugs, migrants from higher-prevalence regions, people with a history of incarceration, patients with HIV or other blood-borne infections, and socially vulnerable populations.

Some of these individuals nevertheless interact repeatedly with primary care, emergency departments, hospitals, laboratories or pharmacy services, leaving potentially informative clinical traces before HCV is suspected.

This hidden reservoir is now regarded as the principal obstacle to elimination, since residual transmission and disease burden concentrate among individuals outside the conventional healthcare circuit or who have never been tested (Romero Otero et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This hidden reservoir is now regarded as the principal obstacle to elimination, since residual transmission and disease burden concentrate among individuals outside the conventional healthcare circuit or who have never been tested <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Romero Otero et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond conventional screening, or opportunistic screening in selected healthcare settings, simple clinical risk scores can improve targeting.

For example, Structured questionnaires and simple risk scores developed for primary care (Martínez-Sanz et al., 2022; McGinn et al., 2008; Nguyen et al., 2005) achieve reasonable discrimination (areas under the curve typically between 0.77 and 0.90), but depend on the availability, completeness, and truthfulness of self-reported risk factors, which are inconsistently captured in daily practice.

text.text: The increasing availability of longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs), administrative claims, laboratory data, prescriptions and healthcare-utilisation histories provides an alternative strategy: identifying high-risk individuals using only information already generated during routine care.

Early large-scale studies using US insurance claims showed that ensemble models could achieve substantially higher precision than universal or risk-based screening at equivalent recall (Doyle et al., 2020), a finding later replicated with gradient-boosting models trained on ambulatory electronic medical records (Rigg et al., 2023).

text.text: Further studies extended this approach by complementing structured EHR variables with risk factors extracted from clinical narratives through natural language processing (Fong et al., 2023; Sánchez-Antolín et al., 2026).

text.text: Large databases produced models with excellent discrimination for high-risk HCV infection among tested individuals (Jang et al., 2025), and some RWD-based models were prospectively deployed in the health system (Dagan et al., 2024).

text.text: Primary-care data from almost two million patients in North-East London also showed that HCV was the most accurately predicted of three blood-borne viruses using routinely recorded demographic, clinical and behavioural indicators (Manley et al., 2026).

text.text: Despite these advances, a recent systematic review identified only 13 HCV prediction models and found substantial heterogeneity, high risk of bias in most studies, scarce primary-care validation and inconsistent reporting (Leber et al., 2025).

text.text: Many models are trained only among tested patients or use a future diagnosis as a proxy for true infection, creating verification and label bias.

Other concerns include temporal leakage, class imbalance, low positive predictive value at population prevalence, limited calibration, and uncertain transportability across health systems and epidemiological contexts.

The present study aimed to develop and validate an interpretable predictor of previously undiagnosed or hidden HCV infection using exclusively routinely collected longitudinal data available within the health system.

By identifying individuals with a high probability of infection without requiring questionnaires, new examinations or additional data collection, this approach seeks to complement existing screening strategies and provide a scalable instrument for the final phase of HCV elimination.

We conducted a retrospective, population-based cohort study to develop and temporally validate a machine-learning model for the identification of undiagnosed (hidden) HCV infection using data routinely collected within the public health system of Andalusia (Southern Spain).

Clinical information was requested to the "Base Poblacional de Salud de Andalucía" (BPS) (Muñoyerro-Muñiz et al., 2020), a regional repository that integrates electronic health records, laboratory results, and diagnostic coding for more than 16 million users of the Andalusian Health system, under the existing regional framework for secure secondary use of health data (Muñoyerro-Muñiz et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Clinical information was requested to the "Base Poblacional de Salud de Andalucía" (BPS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Muñoyerro-Muñiz et al., 2020</ref>), a regional repository that integrates electronic health records, laboratory results, and diagnostic coding for more than 16 million users of the Andalusian Health system, under the existing regional framework for secure secondary use of health data <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Muñoyerro-Muñiz et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: All individuals diagnosed with HCV infection in the BPS between 2017 and 2024 were identified as cases.
A control cohort up to 10 times larger than the case cohort was selected . from the same source population, matched by sex, age, and health district.
Matched controls were assigned the same index date as their corresponding case (the date of HCV diagnosis).
In addition, an independent sample of randomly selected controls was drawn from the BPS, selected independently of the matched case-control dataset and not matched to any individual case.
Eligibility for this independent control group required that individuals be alive throughout 2017-2023.
Each was assigned a random index date within 2024.

Clinical data corresponding to the patients meeting the inclusion criteria was transferred from BPS to the Platform of Generation of Medical Evidence (PAGEM), a Trusted Research Environment for secondary use of clinical data (Muñoyerro-Muñiz et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Clinical data corresponding to the patients meeting the inclusion criteria was transferred from BPS to the Platform of Generation of Medical Evidence (PAGEM), a Trusted Research Environment for secondary use of clinical data <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Muñoyerro-Muñiz et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: All clinical data available in the electronic health record from 30 days prior to the index date to the end of the patient's record, without any additional questionnaire or dedicated data collection, will be used to build the predictor model.

Two domains of variables were considered: (i) chronic diseases and diagnostic history, including hypertension, diabetes, obesity, tobacco dependence, dependence on other substances, chronic liver disease other than cirrhosis, and HIV infection; and (ii) clinical laboratory analytes recorded at any point before the index date (including haemoglobin, alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, gamma-glutamyl transferase, platelet count, and total protein, among others), summarised for each patient using the mean, minimum, maximum, and standard deviation of all available determinations.

The case-control sample was partitioned into training, validation, and test sets using a temporal, non-overlapping criterion based on the year of HCV diagnosis, so that the model was trained exclusively on historical cases and evaluated on progressively more recent, unseen periods.
The training set comprised diagnoses from 2017-2022, the validation set comprised diagnoses from 2023, and the test set comprised diagnoses from 2024.
Two complementary modelling strategies were evaluated.
The first included all available features, whereas the second excluded the income-based pharmaceutical copayment bracket and the area-level socioeconomic index.

The income-based pharmaceutical copayment bracket and the area-level index were removed to reduce the risk of the model primarily capturing socioeconomic disadvantage rather than clinically relevant risk.
For each individual, a single prediction was generated 30 days before the corresponding index date, using only the clinical information available up to that time point.
The index date was defined as the diagnosis date for cases, the matched date for matched controls, and a randomly assigned date for controls in the 2024 test set.
This approach ensured that predictions reflected only information available before the relevant reference date and prevented any post-diagnosis information from contributing to the risk score.

The classification threshold was selected exclusively in the validation set, by requiring a minimum sensitivity (true positive rate) of 60%, prioritising case detection as appropriate for a screening application.
This threshold, together with the aggregation function from which it was derived, was then applied without modification to the independent test set to obtain an unbiased estimate of performance.

To reduce the risk of information leakage and minimise bias related to diagnostic workup immediately preceding hepatitis C diagnosis, a prediction horizon was established 30 days before the index date.
For each individual, only clinical data recorded before this time point was used to generate predictor variables.
The observation window therefore included all available clinical information prior to 30 days before the index date.

This approach was intended to ensure that the model relied on pre-existing clinical information rather than on tests, diagnoses, or healthcare encounters directly associated with the eventual diagnosis of hepatitis C. Alternative prediction horizons were explored in sensitivity analyses to evaluate their impact on model performance.
Candidate predictors were derived from two main sources of clinical information: chronic disease diagnoses and laboratory test results.
Chronic conditions were selected from the information available in the BPS, while laboratory variables were chosen based on their clinical relevance after review by expert hepatologists.
Chronic diseases were encoded as binary variables, indicating whether each condition was present or absent before the prediction horizon.
Laboratory results were processed to capture both the central tendency and longitudinal variability of each biomarker over time.

For each selected laboratory parameter, the following summary features were generated using all available values recorded before the prediction horizon: mean, standard deviation, minimum value, and maximum value.
Sex and age were not included as predictors in the model because they had already been used as matching variables in the matched case-control design.
This decision was made to reduce the possibility that the model would learn patterns driven by the matching procedure rather than clinically meaningful predictors of hepatitis C infection.

Predictive models were developed using an Explainable Boosting Machine (EBM), a generalized-additive-model-based gradient boosting algorithm that combines predictive performance comparable to standard black-box ensembles with feature-level interpretability, allowing the relative contribution of each predictor to the estimated risk to be quantified (Caruana et al., 2015; Nori et al., 2019).

text.text: In this population-based study of the entire Andalusian health system, a machine-learning model built exclusively from structured electronic health record data (including chronic disease diagnoses and longitudinal laboratory summary statistics, without any selfreported risk factor) identified 63.5% of patients who would go on to receive an HCV diagnosis in 2024, at a specificity of 91.8%, with an AUC of 0.837 in this fully independent, population-representative test set (compared with 0.826 in validation and 0.841 in training), indicating that discrimination was well preserved despite the marked change in case-mix between the matched development cohorts and the unmatched test population.

Precision at this operating point was low (7.0%), a direct and expected consequence of evaluating the model against a control population with a true HCV prevalence of approximately 1%, rather than the artificially enriched prevalence of a matched case-control sample.
The negative predictive value, conversely, was high (99.6%).

Predictor importance was dominated by longitudinal liver-related and haematological laboratory markers (alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, platelet count) together with HIV infection, substance dependence, obesity, and a small number of chronic comorbidities, a clinically coherent set of variables, once age, sex, and two variables identified as artefacts of the matched design (two socioeconomic proxies) were removed.
These results presented here extend a rapidly growing body of work applying machine learning to routinely collected health-system data for HCV case-finding.

The most directly comparable efforts used US insurance claims (Doyle et al., 2020) and ambulatory electronic medical records (Rigg et al., 2023), respectively, and reported their models' advantage as a fold-improvement in precision over risk-based or universal screening rather than as a conventional AUC, limiting direct numerical comparison.

text.text: This study presents several characteristics that, taken together, distinguish it from previously published HCV case-finding models.

First, as before, the analysis draws on a genuinely population-scale, multi-year cohort (more than 430,000 individuals across an entire regional health system followed from 2017 to 2024) evaluated under a strict, nonoverlapping temporal split.

Second, and most distinctively, the final test evaluation was deliberately conducted against an independent, non-matched, population-representative control sample rather than the matched controls used for model development.

This is a design choice that directly addresses the verification bias and limited real-world validity (Leber et al., 2025) a drawback of most published models in this field, and which, to our knowledge, few comparable HCV prediction studies have explicitly implemented.

text.text: Third, the exclusion of pharmaceutical co-payment category, and a zone-level deprivation index was not an incidental modelling choice but the outcome of a deliberate bias-auditing step, in which model explainability was used prospectively to detect and remove predictors likely to encode socioeconomic proxies or artefacts of the matched design rather than genuine clinical signal.
This is an equity-oriented methodological safeguard that is largely absent from the prior literature reviewed here.

Fourth, the systematic evaluation of nine prediction horizons spanning 30 to 720 days before diagnosis provides, to our knowledge, the most granular published assessment of how model performance decays with increasing lead time, information directly relevant to designing a realistic screening workflow rather than a single, retrospectively optimal cut-point.

Fifth, formal calibration was assessed and reported transparently, including its limitations, rather than assumed from discrimination alone, a step recommended but rarely implemented in this literature.

Finally, retaining the EBM architecture (Caruana et al., 2015; Nori et al., 2019) preserved full interpretability of the final predictor set throughout this bias-auditing process, which would not have been straightforward with a conventional black-box ensemble, supporting internal consistency across Andalusian health districts, though this remains a withinregion check rather than external validation.

text.text: Obviously, our model is not exempt from limitations.

The low precision (7.0%) and correspondingly high false discovery rate (93.0%) observed at a 60%-sensitivity operating point are an inherent consequence of screening for a low-prevalence condition (~1% in the test population) and would need to be communicated explicitly in any operational deployment, alongside the NNS framing offered above.

Calibration, while modestly improved by isotonic or sigmoid post-hoc adjustment, remained imperfect at higher predicted probabilities in both calibrated and uncalibrated versions, and was not adopted for the primary classification analysis.

Results for the full-variable model and for prediction horizons other than 30 days are reported only in the Supplementary Table 2, limiting the extent to which this model can characterise the trade-off between the excluded variables' predictive contribution and the fairness rationale for their removal.

text.text: Finally, despite this study was conducted entirely within a single regional health system, external validity remains to be established.

Transportability may be limited by differences in EHR coding conventions and laboratory panels across health systems, and by regional differences in the epidemiological profile of undiagnosed HCV (e.g., prevalence of HIV coinfection, injection drug use).

The consistent performance observed across Andalusian health districts (see Results) is reassuring against overfitting to a single local population but remains a within-region check rather than external validation.
Validation in an independent health system, ideally another Spanish region, and eventually beyond Spain, is an essential next step before broader deployment.
